beats.lead: A cease-and-desist order is what actually killed the word "Cab".
beats.text: On 20 October 2010, the San Francisco Metro Transit Authority and the California Public Utilities Commission delivered UberCab a cease-and-desist order.
beats.note: The company was barely four months old; TechCrunch had covered its launch that July.

beats.text: The taxi industry's complaints were specific: no taxi licence, different insurance than licensed taxis, and pickups without the hour's advance booking the law required for limos.
beats.note: Real regulatory objections, not just a turf war.

beats.context: potential jail time threatened for each day UberCab kept operating past the order, on top of a $5,000 fee per instance.

beats.text: The company didn't fight over the name. Within days, UberCab became simply Uber, on its website, its blog, and in a company comment reading "more uber than cab".
beats.note: CEO Ryan Graves told TechCrunch only that the company was working with the agencies to figure out their exact concerns.

beats.text: Because Uber was brand new, it paid for uber.com in company equity rather than cash: shares in a business barely worth anything yet.
beats.note: Universal Music Group held the domain from an unrelated failed venture, then sold its stake early. Fortune reported in 2014 the missed gain topped $100 million.

beats.line: Renamed within days of a cease-and-desist order. The domain deal cost someone else $100 million.
